name: Gandhism
summary: Gandhism is the body of political and social thought drawn from M. K. Gandhi: truth (satya) and nonviolence (ahimsa) as the basis of politics, with means and ends inseparable. It seeks swaraj as self-rule from the village up, in a decentralised economy of simple living, khadi and village industries, and equal status for all, with the wealthy as trustees of their property for the poor. It rejects industrial civilization, class war and State power resting on violence.
scope: Gandhi's own mature writings and programme: Hind Swaraj (1909, with its 1921 preface), the selections edited by Nirmal Kumar Bose (1948), the Constructive Programme (1945 revision) and his trusteeship statements, with an adherents' scholarly collection (Contextualising Gandhian Thought) for context. It excludes later movements that took his name (Bhoodan, Sarvodaya parties, Gandhian socialism as a separate entry) and the Indian National Congress or Indian State's policies, which were not Gandhi's. Statements the texts do not address are null.
